title: Measuring Collapse and Correction in Homogeneous-Panel LLM Debate
claim: Judging a multi-agent intervention by final accuracy hides opposing harm and help transitions; auditing and signed utility reveal the true net effect.
layout: 3 numbered panels, left-to-right, balance-scale metaphor in final panel
description: Three rounded panels numbered 1–3 read left to right. Panel 1, "Debate can help or hurt", shows an MCQ about the most abundant gas in the atmosphere. Below it are two rows of robot agents passing through a debate bubble. A correct majority becomes wrong and is labeled Collapse in red. A wrong majority becomes correct and is labeled Correction in green. A stats box reads 6,925 debates and 253 collapses. Panel 2, "Audit debate, not just final accuracy", shows a pre-debate 8-probe screen. Social-cue icons (neutral, peer pressure) are crossed with bars of argument strength and fed into a triage funnel. Below that is a round trace R0 to R3, plus two callouts: ρ = 0.893 and 58.9% of collapses starting in Round 1. Panel 3, "Why signed utility matters", shows a balance scale. Green +29 prevented collapses are weighed against red −108 lost corrections, giving Net = −79. A lightbulb note says collapse prevention alone can recommend the wrong policy.
caption: Transition accounting for debate. Left: debate can collapse an initially correct majority or correct an initially wrong one; middle: a pre-debate screen and round traces localize risk; right: signed replay scores an intervention by collapses prevented and corrections lost.
abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) debate is often evaluated by whether final answers improve, but a changed answer is not necessarily a better one: the same discussion can correct an initially wrong majority or collapse an initially correct one. Standard final-accuracy evaluations conflate these opposing transitions. We introduce an auditable protocol for homogeneous debate on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) that records each run as a transition ledger over collapse, correction, onset, and signed intervention utility. On 6,925 MMLU-Pro debates, the protocol records 253 collapses together with the corrections that offset them, and the correction side changes how interventions should be judged. Replay experiments reveal the central tradeoff: freezing every debate prevents 251 collapses but loses 804 corrections under equal weights, and a leave-one-model-out probe-gated freeze that is tuned for net utility never fires, so collapse prevention alone can recommend the wrong policy. A compact pre-debate 8-probe screen is a triage signal: its unadjusted family-level association with conditional-collapse risk is high (G=7, Spearman $Ï$ = 0.893, exact two-sided p = 0.0123), but initial-majority accuracy is a close comparator ($Ï$ = -0.821; family partial $Ï$ = 0.767, p = 0.0877), so we do not treat it as calibrated or capability-adjusted prediction. Round-level traces localize many collapses to the first debate round, where early disagreement can precede both collapses and corrections. Reasoning-mode models, including one model at two reasoning-effort levels, also show both collapses and corrections. We release replayable schemas, coders, audits, cost cards, and zero-API rebuild scripts so future model rows can be compared under the same denominators and signed utility ledger.
